text.p: Global Depositary Receipts of Lebanon's biggest company Solidere soared on the London Stock Exchange on Tuesday and the company said it believed purchases by international emerging market funds were behind the increase.

The GDRs, issued in November at $11.50, jumped to $17.625 from last week's $12. That was 70 percent above the current price of the underlying A shares which traded on the Beirut Stock Exchange on Tuesday at $10.375.
"There is definitely a big buyer buying the GDRs," a dealer for a major London bank told Reuters in Beirut by telephone. "We want to know why he's ready to pay this premium."

The underlying A shares rose on the Beirut Stock Exchange on Tuesday for the first time since April 2, reaching $10.375 from $10.25, and brokers said the rise appeared linked to the increase in the London price of the GDRs.

Asked about the GDR movement, a Solidere official said he believed international institutional investors, who are barred from buying the underlying shares, were buying the GDRs after visiting Beirut to inspect the company's progress in its 25-year programme to rebuild the city centre.

David Mulville, who heads Solidere's stock management department, said the company had been bringing groups of investors to Beirut since the beginning of the year to show them the progress it was making in what it has billed as the biggest urban renewal project of the 1990s.
"We've been getting as many as possible to come and see what is happening," Mulville said.
The latest group of investors brought to Beirut last week by a major European investment bank comprised U.S. and European emerging market fund managers, he said.
Asked if the GDR purchases were linked to the visits by institutional investors, Mulville said: "I would have thought so."
"I don't know the identity of the buyers but I can make the safe assumption that investors have been buying as a result of trips to Beirut and to the Middle East region," he added.
He was not able to identify the institutions which had come to Beirut and would not speculate about why investors should buy the GDRs at a large premium to the underlying shares.
However, a Beirut financial source noted that several recent research documents by international and local financial houses estimated that the shares were trading at a steep discount.
A Merrill Lynch research this year put their value at around $20.

"Investors realise that the under-valuation of the local shares is due to a technical factor -- the current over-supply of A shares -- and they are longterm investors looking for five years or so," the financial source said.
"Also, there is a certain scarcity value to the GDRs because the size of the programme was limited and these investors know they are still buying them at a discount to the real value," he added.
"They are comfortable that the price is relatively cheap having seen what is happening here on the ground."
Mulville told Reuters he believed Solidere was beginning to benefit from an increase this year in investor interest in the Middle East.

"These groups of investors have also been visiting other countries in the region like Egypt where share trading has developed hugely this year...and I think we are beginning to see the same phenomenon here despite the fact that the underlying Solidere shares are lower," Mulville said.
